about: Run 2026-11-11-exact-integers, THE PROBE and THE WALK (tools/integer_probe.py): a call that floors or rounds a real value on purpose, as the check's own definition. Each entry is {"site": <a site key, as tools/integer_probe.py writes one>, "why": <why the check's own definition floors or rounds there>, "test": "tests/<file>.py::<function>", a test whose fractional input reads as the check should}. Neither measure counts a finding at a named site. No site the probe finds receiving an injected value itself may be named here: such a site reads through THE RULE. Empty at the base (step measure); step fix-a2 names the eight roundings in number_theory's Riemann checks, and step fix-b the twenty in the other files (Meeus's calendar floors, the ceilings of counts of whole things, a repeat count, the Riemann-Siegel table size), each of a real value the check computes, none of an integer the spec writes.

fields.why: The Riemann-Siegel formula sums to N = floor(sqrt(t / 2 pi)) of the real height t and corrects by the fraction q = a - N it leaves: the floor is the formula's own.
The scan's grid over the real span from start to b, a step h apart, holds ceil((b - start) / h) + 1 points, the last one clipped to b: the grid's own count.
The argument principle's step count grows by one for each 400 of the real height T: a schedule of the computation, never a reading of the claim.
N(T), the strip count computed as a real number, must land within 0.05 of an integer; the nearest integer is what it is tested against.
The zeros the line must hold are the integer the computed real strip count N(T) lands on.
Where the line scan falls short, the zeros a span must hold are the integer the difference of two computed real strip counts lands on (this branch runs only on a shortfall).
The check refuses a computed real strip count N(T) that does not land within 0.05 of an integer.
The zeros in the strip are the integer the computed real strip count N(T) lands on.
Occupants are the floor area over the load factor rounded up: a part of a person's share still needs a whole person's room. The ceiling is the check's own formula.
The power formula gives a real n; a group of fewer whole subjects than it falls short, so the required n is its ceiling, plus one.
A repeat count is whole: the whole number of measuring windows the last run fits in, plus one.
Cans are the area over one can's coverage rounded up: a part of a can is bought as a can. The ceiling is the check's own formula.
Tiles are the area over one tile rounded up: a cut tile is a whole tile. The ceiling is the check's own formula.
The waste allowance adds a real share of tiles, bought as whole tiles: the check's own ceiling.
Meeus's Julian Day (Astronomical Algorithms, ch. 7): A = floor(Y / 100), the algorithm's own floor.
Meeus ch. 7: B = 2 - A + floor(A / 4), the Gregorian correction's own floor.
Meeus ch. 7: floor(365.25 (Y + 4716)), the days of the years, the algorithm's own floor.
Meeus ch. 7: floor(30.6001 (M + 1)), the days of the months, the algorithm's own floor.
Meeus ch. 7, calendar date from JD: Z, the integer part of JD + 0.5, and F its fraction.
Meeus ch. 7: alpha = floor((Z - 1867216.25) / 36524.25), the Gregorian centuries' own floor.
Meeus ch. 7: A = Z + 1 + alpha - floor(alpha / 4), the algorithm's own floor.
Meeus ch. 7: C = floor((B - 122.1) / 365.25), the year count's own floor.
Meeus ch. 7: D = floor(365.25 C), the days of those years, the algorithm's own floor.
Meeus ch. 7: E = floor((B - D) / 30.6001), the month count's own floor.
Meeus ch. 7: the day is B - D - floor(30.6001 E) + F, the algorithm's own floor.
The calendar day is the whole day the real day count falls in: an ISO date names no fraction of a day.
Par is the gross-up rounded up to the issuance step: the check's own definition, so the net proceeds are always covered.
The C backend's table runs one past floor(sqrt(tmax / 2 pi)), the longest Riemann-Siegel main sum below tmax: the formula's own floor.
